title: Refining the Architecture of the Quadruple Pre-main-sequence System HD 98800: Improved Orbits, Dynamical Masses, and a Transiting Circumbinary Disk
comment: 21 pages including figures and tables. Accepted for publication in The Astrophysical Journal
summary: We present new spectroscopic and interferometric observations of the pre-main-sequence hierarchical quadruple system HD 98800, a member of the nearby TW Hya association. Our radial velocity monitoring extends the total coverage to over 36 years, sampling the periastron passage in the $\sim$240-yr outer orbit. By combining these velocities with new and archival interferometric observations of both inner binaries (A and B), we significantly refine the system orbits and constrain the dynamical masses of all four stars to $\leq$ 2.6 percent. The resulting stellar properties (masses, effective temperatures, and absolute magnitudes) are found to agree well with current stellar evolution models. Notably, binary B hosts a known circumbinary disk in a polar orientation. Our interferometric imaging, as well as ground-based photometry by others, capture binary A currently passing directly behind the disk, a striking alignment given the outer orbit's long period. We use the photometry to infer the optical extinction produced by the disk material. The eclipse is expected to last about a decade, and offers an unprecedented opportunity to probe the structure and composition of the potentially planet-forming disk. Our refined orbits and component masses provide a robust dynamical framework to support ongoing and future studies of this unique event.

AI.tldr: New spectroscopy and interferometry of the HD 98800 quadruple system refine all orbital elements and dynamical masses of the four stars to ≤2.6%, validate stellar evolution models, and capture binary A transiting behind binary B's polar circumbinary disk—a decade-long eclipse ideal for probing disk structure and composition.
AI.motivation: HD 98800 is a nearby hierarchical quadruple pre-main-sequence system in the TW Hya association, and its binary B hosts a polar circumbinary disk; precise orbits and masses are needed to interpret the system and to exploit the rare chance to study the disk via occultation.
AI.method: Long-baseline radial velocity monitoring extended to >36 yr, covering periastron of the ~240-yr outer orbit, combined with new and archival interferometric observations of both inner binaries (A and B) to jointly fit orbits; photometry used to infer optical extinction from the disk.
AI.result: System orbits significantly refined; dynamical masses of all four stars constrained to ≤2.6%; masses, effective temperatures, and absolute magnitudes agree with current evolutionary models. Binary A is observed passing directly behind the polar circumbinary disk of B, with extinction measured and an eclipse duration of about a decade.
AI.conclusion: The refined orbits and component masses provide a robust dynamical framework, and the ongoing ~decade eclipse offers an unprecedented opportunity to probe the structure and composition of a potentially planet-forming disk.

title: A Meta-analysis of Chemical Abundances Derived from Ultraviolet and Optical Lines of Os, Ir, and Pt, and a Reassessment of the Robustness of the Third r-process Peak in Metal-poor Stars
comment: Accepted for publication in the Astrophysical Journal (19 pages, 7 figures, 4 tables)
summary: We reassess the abundance ratio between elements at the third rapid neutron-capture process (r-process) peak (Os, Ir, Pt) and the lanthanide element Eu. We show that some weak optical lines of Os I, Ir I, and Pt I yield abundances inconsistent with stronger ultraviolet (UV) and optical lines and provide recommendations for their limited use alongside more reliable lines. We perform a meta-analysis of Os, Ir, and Pt abundances from 35 studies of 77 r-process-enhanced metal-poor stars spanning -3.43 < [Fe/H] < -1.27 and +0.22 < [Eu/Fe] < +2.45. The mean third-peak to lanthanide abundance ratios are $\log\varepsilon$(Os/Eu) = 0.86 $\pm$ 0.02, $\log\varepsilon$(Ir/Eu) = 0.88 $\pm$ 0.03, and $\log\varepsilon$(Pt/Eu) = 1.12 $\pm$ 0.04, which agree with the inferred Solar System r-process ratios to within 0.05 dex. These abundance ratios vary by less than 0.50 dex (a factor of 3.2), 0.56 dex (a factor of 3.6), and 0.45 dex (a factor of 2.8), respectively, in 90 percent of the r-process events that enriched metal-poor stars in existing samples. We use a representative r-process model to show that the small range of stellar abundance ratios favor models with a substantial contribution from neutron-rich material, with electron fractions, $Y_e$, < 0.2. We conclude that the third-peak to lanthanide abundance ratios are robust in existing r-process-enhanced star samples. In two stars with [Eu/Fe] < 0, the upper limits derived from non-detection of Pt indicate that the third-peak elements are deficient relative to lanthanides, and we conclude that this may be a signature of the limited r-process.

AI.tldr: Reanalysis of third r-process peak (Os, Ir, Pt) versus Eu abundances across 77 metal-poor stars confirms ratios matching Solar System r-process values, supporting r-process models with neutron-rich ejecta (Ye < 0.2).
AI.motivation: The abundance ratio between the third r-process peak elements (Os, Ir, Pt) and lanthanides (e.g., Eu) is a key diagnostic of r-process conditions, but prior stellar abundance measurements have been inconsistent and subject to unreliable line data, motivating a rigorous reassessment.
AI.method: The authors identify that some weak optical lines of Os I, Ir I, and Pt I yield abundances inconsistent with stronger UV and optical lines and recommend caution with those lines. They then perform a meta-analysis of Os, Ir, and Pt abundances from 35 studies of 77 r-process-enhanced metal-poor stars (-3.43 < [Fe/H] < -1.27, +0.22 < [Eu/Fe] < +2.45), and compare the resulting ratios with Solar System r-process values and with a representative r-process model.
AI.result: Mean third-peak-to-Eu ratios are log ε(Os/Eu) = 0.86 ± 0.02, log ε(Ir/Eu) = 0.88 ± 0.03, and log ε(Pt/Eu) = 1.12 ± 0.04, agreeing with inferred Solar System r-process ratios within 0.05 dex. The ratios vary by less than 0.50, 0.56, and 0.45 dex (factors of ~3.2, 3.6, 2.8) in 90% of the r-process events. The narrow spread favors models with substantial neutron-rich material (Ye < 0.2). In two stars with [Eu/Fe] < 0, Pt non-detections imply third-peak elements are deficient relative to lanthanides.
AI.conclusion: Third-peak-to-lanthanide abundance ratios are robust in existing r-process-enhanced star samples and consistent with Solar System r-process values. The small observed scatter supports neutron-rich (Ye < 0.2) r-process models, and the deficiency of third-peak elements relative to lanthanides in [Eu/Fe] < 0 stars may signal a limited r-process.

title: Multi-vantage SO/PHI and SDO/HMI magnetic field observations of active region NOAA 13465
comment: Accepted to A&A
summary:
Context. Until the launch of Solar Orbiter, long term studies of active region magnetic fields were restricted to a single vantage point: that from Earth. What further restricted these studies were geometrical effects, such as foreshortening and projection, that plague magnetic field observations when the active region was away from the central meridian.
  Aims. To track an active region, in this case NOAA 13465, with Solar Orbiter during a perihelion pass and use co-observations made by SDO/HMI and SO/PHI-HRT from different vantage points to explore the systematics plaguing observations away from disc centre.
  Methods. We use the SHARP (Space-Weather HMI Active Region Patches) data series from SDO/HMI, and create similar datasets with SO/PHI-HRT observations. We compare and contrast the line-of-sight and the three heliographic magnetic field components. Finally we compare the unsigned radial flux, and unsigned totals of the northward and westward magnetic components using the SHARP masking method to select a common area.
  Results. We find that the instrument observing closer to the limb infers a greater unsigned radial magnetic flux compared to that observing at disc centre, with a maximum near approximately $45^\circ$. The plage displayed more susceptibility to resolution and projection effects than the active region's sole sunspot. In particular the deduced area of the solar plage drove the observed increase in flux near the limb. Thanks to its higher spatial resolution, the SO/PHI-HRT data showed a smaller effect compared to SDO/HMI near the limb, highlighting a dependence on instrument resolution. Finally, the ratio of the two instruments' vertical magnetic flux exhibits a strong positive correlation with the ratio of the cosine of the instruments' viewing angles.

AI.tldr: Tracking NOAA 13465 with Solar Orbiter and SDO/HMI from different vantage points reveals that limb-nearer observations infer greater unsigned radial flux (peaking near ~45°), driven mainly by plage area rather than sunspot effects, with dependence on instrument resolution.
AI.motivation: Long-term active region magnetic field studies have historically relied on a single vantage point (Earth), and were further limited by geometrical effects like foreshortening and projection that plague observations away from disc centre. Solar Orbiter enables multi-vantage-point co-observations to systematically explore these perspective-dependent biases.
AI.method: The active region NOAA 13465 was tracked with Solar Orbiter during a perihelion pass, using co-observations from SDO/HMI and SO/PHI-HRT at different viewing angles. SHARP data series from HMI were used, and analogous datasets were constructed from PHI-HRT observations. Line-of-sight and three heliographic magnetic field components were compared, along with unsigned radial flux and unsigned totals of the northward and westward components, selecting a common area via the SHARP masking method.
AI.result: The instrument observing closer to the limb inferred a greater unsigned radial magnetic flux than the disc-centre observer, with a maximum near ~45°. The plage was more susceptible to resolution and projection effects than the single sunspot; the deduced plage area drove the flux increase near the limb. Due to higher spatial resolution, PHI-HRT showed a smaller effect than HMI near the limb, indicating a dependence on instrument resolution. The ratio of vertical magnetic fluxes between instruments correlated strongly and positively with the ratio of the cosines of their viewing angles.
AI.conclusion: Perspective/geometrical effects introduce viewing-angle-dependent biases in active region magnetic flux estimates, dominated by projected plage area and modulated by instrument resolution. These findings are important for interpreting single-vantage-point long-term studies and for cross-calibrating magnetic field measurements from Solar Orbiter and Earth-based observatories.

title: The Eclipsing $γ$ Doradus Star VZ Canum Venaticorum
comment: 9 pages, including 4 figures and 3 tables, accepted for publication in PASJ
summary: We present a detailed analysis of the eclipsing binary VZ CVn using TESS Sectors 50 and 77 photometry together with published spectroscopic results. The TESS light curves were modeled to refine the binary parameters, and the residual light curves were analyzed to investigate the pulsational properties of the system. We derive masses and radii of $M_{\rm A}=1.526\pm0.005$ $M_\odot$ and $R_{\rm A}=1.638\pm0.023$ $R_\odot$ for the primary and $M_{\rm B}=1.259\pm0.005$ $M_\odot$ and $R_{\rm B}=1.133\pm0.016$ $R_\odot$ for the secondary. Comparison with PARSEC evolutionary models suggests a near-solar metallicity of $Z=0.017$ and an age of 1.0 Gyr. Separate frequency analyses of the two TESS sectors reveal four signals with possible counterparts in both sectors. Two of these frequencies, $f_2=4.7486$ day$^{-1}$ and $f_6=7.1242$ day$^{-1}$, are consistent with the fourth and sixth orbital harmonics, respectively, suggesting an orbital origin rather than independent $δ$ Sct pulsations. The dominant frequency $f_1=1.7577$ day$^{-1}$ has a pulsation constant of $Q_1=0.336$ day, consistent with a $γ$ Dor-type g-mode pulsation. The weaker signal $f_5=1.9754$ day$^{-1}$ also has a pulsation constant of $Q_5=0.299$ day, although its detection remains tentative because of its low S/N. Together with the physical and evolutionary properties of the primary, these results support its classification as a $γ$ Dor pulsator rather than the previously proposed $γ$ Dor--$δ$ Sct hybrid pulsator.

AI.tldr: TESS photometry of VZ CVn yields refined binary parameters and reveals the primary to be a γ Dor pulsator, not a γ Dor–δ Sct hybrid.
AI.motivation: To refine the physical parameters of the eclipsing binary VZ CVn and to re-evaluate the previously proposed classification of its primary as a γ Dor–δ Sct hybrid pulsator using high-precision space photometry.
AI.method: Uses TESS Sectors 50 and 77 photometry with published spectroscopy. The light curves are modeled to refine binary parameters; residual light curves are frequency-analyzed per sector to characterize pulsations, with pulsation constants (Q) and harmonic checks against the orbital frequency. Comparison with PARSEC evolutionary models constrains metallicity and age.
AI.result: Primary: M_A = 1.526 ± 0.005 M⊙, R_A = 1.638 ± 0.023 R⊙. Secondary: M_B = 1.259 ± 0.005 M⊙, R_B = 1.133 ± 0.016 R⊙. PARSEC fit: Z = 0.017 (near-solar), age ≈ 1.0 Gyr. Four frequencies recovered with possible counterparts in both sectors; f2 = 4.7486 d⁻¹ and f6 = 7.1242 d⁻¹ match the 4th and 6th orbital harmonics (orbital origin). Dominant f1 = 1.7577 d⁻¹ has Q1 = 0.336 d (γ Dor g-mode); f5 = 1.9754 d⁻¹ has Q5 = 0.299 d but is tentative (low S/N).
AI.conclusion: Combined with the primary's physical and evolutionary properties, the results support classifying the primary as a γ Dor pulsator rather than a γ Dor–δ Sct hybrid.

title: Spectroscopic identification of z>7 quasars with Roman Space Telescope
comment: 13 pages, 5 figures. Revised manuscript resubmitted to ApJ following a positive referee report
summary: The Roman Wide Field Instrument grism will cover a large area over 1.0-1.93 micrometers, making it possible to search directly for Lyman-alpha breaks in quasars beyond redshift z = 7. We simulate quasars at z = 7.5-10 under HLWAS-like exposures with ESpRESSO, including PSF convolution, slitless dispersion, source and background Poisson noise, read noise, and Horne optimal extraction. Three Lyman-alpha equivalent-width (EW) prescriptions are used to bracket the uncertainty in line strength, and the extracted spectra are compared with M/L/T dwarfs and passive red galaxies using the spectral angle mapper. The Lyman-alpha-break completeness remains above 90% to J_AB approximately 23.7-24.1 and reaches 50% at J_AB approximately 24.3-24.7. Beyond J_AB approximately 25, the result depends strongly on the adopted EW distribution. In the fixed-redshift SAM test, the QSO recovery rate is TPR >= 0.982. None of the noisy brown-dwarf or red-galaxy test spectra is classified as a QSO. Because those test spectra are generated from the same finite parent libraries as the reference classes, this result measures the stability of the classification against noise within those libraries rather than an independently calibrated survey false-positive rate. At the faint end, the strongest astrophysical sensitivity in the present calculation is to the high-EW tail of the Lyman-alpha distribution.

AI.tldr: Simulations show that Roman's Wide Field Instrument grism can detect Lyman-alpha breaks in z=7.5-10 quasars, with >90% completeness down to J_AB~23.7-24.1, though faint-end performance depends critically on the assumed Lyman-alpha EW distribution.
AI.motivation: Roman's WFI grism spans 1.0-1.93 microns over a large area, enabling a direct search for Lyman-alpha breaks in quasars at z>7. This work quantifies the feasibility and completeness of such a search.
AI.method: The authors simulate z=7.5-10 quasars under HLWAS-like exposures with ESpRESSO, modeling PSF convolution, slitless dispersion, source and background Poisson noise, read noise, and Horne optimal extraction. Three Lyman-alpha equivalent-width prescriptions bracket line-strength uncertainty. Extracted spectra are classified against M/L/T dwarfs and passive red galaxies using a spectral angle mapper.
AI.result: Lyman-alpha-break completeness stays above 90% to J_AB~23.7-24.1 and drops to 50% at J_AB~24.3-24.7; beyond J_AB~25 results depend strongly on the EW distribution. In the fixed-redshift SAM test the QSO recovery rate is TPR>=0.982, and no noisy brown-dwarf or red-galaxy spectrum is misclassified as a QSO.
AI.conclusion: The grism search is viable to J_AB~24, but the faint-end sensitivity is dominated by the high-EW tail of the Lyman-alpha distribution. Because test spectra derive from the same parent libraries as the reference classes, the zero-false-positive result reflects classification stability under noise rather than an independently calibrated survey false-positive rate.

title: A Wideband Technosignature Search of 210,191 Nearby Main-sequence Stars with the VLA Sky Survey
comment: 30 pages, 9 figures. Submitted to AAS Journals
summary: Searches for radio technosignatures have concentrated on narrowband signals. We present a complementary search for excess broadband 2-4 GHz emission from 210,191 Gaia DR3 main-sequence stars within 100 pc in all epochs of the VLA Sky Survey (VLASS; 2017-2026). Cross-matching with the Epoch-1 catalog yields 51 high-reliability positional associations (versus 1.5 expected by chance). All but one are known natural emitters that, where measurable, move with their stars; the remaining source, near LSPM J1943+5337, is not at the star. Because stellar flares can mimic transmitters in continuum flux, a detection counts as a possible transmitter at any luminosity only at the 32,985 apparently single AFGK stars outside known radio-emitter classes, and at M dwarfs and AFGK multiples only above $10^{10}$ W Hz$^{-1}$. Forced photometry of 208,232 stars in all epochs finds 1 steady-test detection and 3 stars detected in at least one epoch among the eligible stars, against 1.3 and 1.9 expected by chance. The median per-star limit on steady emission is $L_ν<4.0\times10^{8}$ W Hz$^{-1}$. Without background subtraction, fewer than $1.5\times10^{-4}$ of eligible AFGK stars host a steady transmitter above $10^9$ W Hz$^{-1}$, and fewer than $2.3\times10^{-5}$ of all stars outside the known-emitter classes host one above $\sim1.1\times10^{10}$ W Hz$^{-1}$; counting every M-dwarf detection as a possible transmitter, fewer than $5.5\times10^{-4}$ of M dwarfs host one above $10^9$ W Hz$^{-1}$. Stacks detect population-averaged emission from M dwarfs, concentrated in those with activity evidence. Continuum surveys thus constrain broadband, modulated, or rapidly drifting signals that narrowband pipelines do not search for.

AI.tldr: A complementary broadband (2-4 GHz) technosignature search using all VLASS epochs toward 210,191 nearby Gaia DR3 main-sequence stars finds no credible excess emission, and places tight upper limits on the fraction of stars hosting steady broadband transmitters.
AI.motivation: Prior radio technosignature searches have focused almost exclusively on narrowband signals, leaving broadband, modulated, or rapidly drifting emission largely unconstrained. The authors aim to fill this gap with a continuum-based search that complements narrowband pipelines.
AI.method: Cross-match 210,191 Gaia DR3 main-sequence stars within 100 pc against all VLASS epochs (2017-2026), yielding 51 high-reliability positional associations in Epoch 1. Define conservative eligibility criteria to exclude natural emitters: apparent single AFGK stars outside known radio-emitter classes count at any luminosity, while M dwarfs and AFGK multiples count only above 1e10 W/Hz. Perform forced photometry on 208,232 stars across all epochs, compute chance-coincidence expectations, derive per-star luminosity limits, and stack sources to probe population-averaged emission, including separation by activity indicators.
AI.result: Of 51 associations, all but one are known natural emitters that move with their stars; the remaining source near LSPM J1943+5337 is offset from the star. Forced photometry finds 1 steady-test detection and 3 stars detected in at least one epoch among eligible stars (vs. 1.3 and 1.9 expected by chance). The median per-star limit is L_nu < 4.0e8 W/Hz. Upper limits: <1.5e-4 of eligible AFGK stars host a steady transmitter above 1e9 W/Hz; <2.3e-5 of all stars outside known-emitter classes host one above ~1.1e10 W/Hz; <5.5e-4 of M dwarfs host one above 1e9 W/Hz. Stacks detect population-averaged emission from M dwarfs, concentrated in those with activity evidence.
AI.conclusion: Continuum VLA surveys provide strong, quantitative constraints on broadband, modulated, or rapidly drifting technosignatures that narrowband searches cannot detect, demonstrating the value of continuum surveys as a complement to traditional narrowband SETI. No credible broadband transmitter candidates were identified among nearby main-sequence stars.

title: JWST/NIRSpec observations of AMORE6 suggest active Pop~III star formation in a self-polluted galaxy
comment: Comments are welcome
summary: AMORE6 is a strongly lensed ($μ\simeq78$), intrinsically faint galaxy at $z=5.725$, previously proposed as a metal-free candidate from the absence of [OIII]$λ$5007 in NIRCam slitless spectroscopy. We present deep JWST/NIRSpec spectroscopy of its brighter image, AMORE6-B. We detect HeII$λλ$1640,4686, with HeII$λ$4686/H$β=0.080\pm0.015$ and EW(HeII$λ$4686)$=35\pm8$ Å, weak [OIII] ($R_3=0.25$) and CIV$λλ$1548,51, and no other metal lines. H and He lines give negligible attenuation, $T_e\simeq2\times10^4$ K, and $Y=0.226^{+0.022}_{-0.024}$. The oxygen abundance, $12+\log(O/H)\simeq6.08^{+0.24}_{-0.80}$ (0.04-0.4% $Z_\odot$, depending on the calibration), is the lowest at its stellar mass, while C/O is near or above solar. Photoionization models of different ionizing sources favour metal-free stars with a top-heavy initial mass function (IMF), as in the self-polluted phase of simulated Population III (Pop III) galaxies, or a metal-poor population with a luminous hard X-ray source; ordinary metal-poor populations, very massive stars, and accretion-based sources are disfavoured. A full SED fit in the fiducial self-polluted scenario gives $1.3\times10^5\,M_\odot$ of Pop III stars formed within the last 4 Myr, which ionize mildly enriched gas and leak 86% of their ionizing photons. The HeII-to-Balmer ratio constrains the slope $x$ and characteristic mass $M_{ch}$ of the Pop III IMF jointly, to $90x-268\lesssim M_{ch}/M_\odot\lesssim172x-330$ ($3σ$; $M_{ch}\lesssim70\,M_\odot$ for a Salpeter slope), excluding the most top-heavy IMFs allowed by near-field constraints. X-ray binaries are a possible alternative, but require either a metal-poor population too young (1 Myr) to host compact objects and an X-ray luminosity far above that of metal-poor galaxies, or $2\times10^6\,M_\odot$ of older Pop III.2 stars whose metals were mostly expelled.

AI.tldr: JWST/NIRSpec spectroscopy of the strongly lensed (μ≈78), intrinsically faint z=5.725 galaxy AMORE6-B confirms an extremely low oxygen abundance (12+log(O/H)≈6.08, 0.04–0.4% Z⊙) and HeII emission consistent with metal-free, top-heavy Pop III-like stars, though with a smaller characteristic mass than near-field constraints allow.
AI.motivation: AMORE6 was proposed as a metal-free candidate from the absence of [OIII]λ5007 in NIRCam slitless spectroscopy. The authors aim to verify this with deep spectroscopy and to constrain the ionizing source and stellar population.
AI.method: Deep JWST/NIRSpec spectroscopy of the brighter lensed image AMORE6-B; measurement of HeII, Hβ, [OIII], and CIV line strengths; derivation of attenuation, Te, Y, O/H and C/O; photoionization modeling of candidate ionizing sources; full SED fitting in a self-polluted Pop III scenario; joint constraints on Pop III IMF slope x and characteristic mass Mch from the HeII-to-Balmer ratio.
AI.result: Detections of HeIIλλ1640,4686 (HeIIλ4686/Hβ=0.080±0.015, EW=35±8 Å), weak [OIII] (R3=0.25) and CIVλλ1548,51, with no other metal lines. Negligible attenuation, Te≈2×10^4 K, Y=0.226(+0.022/−0.024), O/H≈6.08(+0.24/−0.80), C/O near or above solar. Models favor metal-free stars with a top-heavy IMF (self-polluted Pop III phase) or a metal-poor population with a hard X-ray source. Fiducial fit: 1.3×10^5 M⊙ of Pop III stars formed in last 4 Myr, 86% ionizing photon leakage. IMF constraint: 90x−268 ≲ Mch/M⊙ ≲ 172x−330 (3σ; Mch≲70 M⊙ for Salpeter).
AI.conclusion: AMORE6-B is the lowest-metallicity object at its stellar mass and its emission is best explained by recent, metal-free top-heavy Pop III star formation (or an X-ray-binary alternative requiring extreme conditions). The HeII/Balmer ratio excludes the most top-heavy IMFs permitted by near-field constraints; ordinary metal-poor populations, very massive stars, and accretion-based sources are disfavored.

title: Quiet-Sun magnetic field configuration inferred from the ratio of longitudinal fields measured in the Fe I λ6301 and λ6302 Å lines
summary: The estimate of the longitudinal magnetic field obtained from the Hinode spectropolarimeter data will be different if it is determined in different ways. In particular, the values obtained by the Center Of Gravity (COG) method for the Fe I $λ$ 6301 and 6302 $Å$ lines do not coincide. Some of the differences are due to the different inaccuracies of the COG method for each of the two lines. However, some of the differences can be explained by the fact that the response functions of these lines to changes in the magnetic field are formed at different heights. This should be accompanied by a certain morphological structure of magnetic fields. It consists in the fact that most of the magnetic configurations of the quiet photosphere are similar to each other. To a rough approximation, their structure can be compared with the structure of a sunspot - there is a central region with the strongest field, close to vertical, and slopes - an analog of penumbra, where the field weakens and / or turns to horizontal. This turn occurs at the heights of the greatest response of the Fe I $λ$ 6301 and 6302 $Å$ lines to changes in the magnetic field with a turn length of about tens of kilometers.

AI.tldr: Longitudinal magnetic field estimates from Hinode spectropolarimeter data differ depending on the determination method; discrepancies between the COG results for Fe I 6301 and 6302 Å arise partly from differing line-specific COG inaccuracies and partly because the two lines respond to field changes at different heights, implying a common morphological magnetic structure in the quiet photosphere.
AI.motivation: To explain why longitudinal field strengths derived from Hinode spectropolarimetric data differ between methods, specifically between the COG estimates for the Fe I 6301 and 6302 Å lines, and to identify the physical cause of these discrepancies.
AI.method: Analysis of Hinode spectropolarimeter data using the Center of Gravity method applied separately to the Fe I 6301 and 6302 Å lines; comparison of the resulting longitudinal field estimates and interpretation via the response functions of each line to magnetic field changes at different atmospheric heights.
AI.result: The COG values for the two lines do not coincide. Part of the difference is attributable to differing inaccuracies of the COG method for each line, while part reflects the fact that the response functions of the two lines to field changes form at different heights.
AI.conclusion: The height-dependent response of the two Fe I lines implies a characteristic magnetic morphology: most quiet-photosphere magnetic configurations resemble a sunspot, with a central near-vertical strong-field region and penumbra-like sloped surroundings where the field weakens and/or turns horizontal. This turning occurs at the heights of maximum response of the Fe I 6301 and 6302 Å lines, with a turn length of order tens of kilometers.

title: AGN feedback in the multiphase inner intracluster medium of a cosmological super-resolved galaxy cluster
comment: Submitted to MNRAS, 19 pages, 13 figures
summary: The intracluster medium (ICM) of galaxy cluster cores is a multiphase environment regulated by active galactic nuclei (AGN) feedback. Extended cool gas nebulae with complex morphologies and kinematics are commonly observed in cool-core clusters, but their origin and interaction with AGN feedback remain poorly understood. We present a cosmological magnetohydrodynamical zoom-in simulation of a low-mass cool-core galaxy cluster ($M_{\mathrm{200c}}=2.3\times10^{14}\,\mathrm{M}_\odot$), using initial conditions from TNG-Cluster and the IllustrisTNG galaxy formation model. Through super-Lagrangian refinement, we achieve a baryonic mass resolution of $2.3\times10^{4}\,\mathrm{M}_\odot$ and a spatial resolution of $\sim40\text{-}90$ pc in the cool ($10^{4}\,\mathrm{K}<T<10^{5.5}\,\mathrm{K}$) gas phase within the central $370$ ckpc, while retaining the full cosmological context. We investigate the properties and evolution of cool clouds and filaments and their interaction with AGN feedback at $z\leq0.35$. The cluster core hosts a rich population of dense, low-entropy filaments, including inflowing and outflowing structures and occasional rotationally supported disks. Comparing simulations with AGN kinetic feedback turned off and on, we find that AGN activity fragments and redistributes the cool gas and increases its covering fraction without destroying the cool gas reservoir. Individual outbursts drive transient increases in the velocities and velocity dispersions of both cool and hot gas, on short, $\lesssim 50$ Myr, timescales. We also identify low-entropy gas uplifted by AGN-driven outflows. While feedback globally heats the ICM and offsets cooling, it also creates conditions that may favor local thermal instabilities -- through shock compressions, mixing, turbulence, and uplift.

AI.tldr: A high-resolution cosmological MHD zoom-in simulation of a low-mass cool-core cluster shows that AGN kinetic feedback fragments and redistributes cool gas, boosts its covering fraction and velocity dispersion on short timescales, and generates turbulence/mixing/uplift that can locally trigger thermal instabilities, while globally heating the ICM and preserving the cool gas reservoir.
AI.motivation: Extended cool gas nebulae with complex morphology and kinematics are common in cool-core clusters, yet their origin and interaction with AGN feedback are poorly understood. The authors aim to resolve the multiphase ICM and directly study how AGN feedback shapes cool clouds and filaments.
AI.method: Cosmological magnetohydrodynamical zoom-in simulation of a low-mass cool-core cluster (M200c = 2.3e14 Msun) using TNG-Cluster initial conditions and the IllustrisTNG model. Super-Lagrangian refinement yields baryonic mass resolution of 2.3e4 Msun and ~40-90 pc spatial resolution in the cool (1e4 K < T < 1e5.5 K) phase within the central 370 ckpc, retaining full cosmological context. Cool cloud/filament properties and AGN interaction analyzed at z <= 0.35, with AGN kinetic feedback toggled on/off.
AI.result: The core hosts dense, low-entropy filaments—inflowing, outflowing, and occasionally rotationally supported disks. AGN activity fragments and redistributes cool gas and raises its covering fraction without destroying the reservoir. Individual outbursts cause transient (<~50 Myr) increases in velocities and velocity dispersion of cool and hot gas. Low-entropy gas uplifted by AGN outflows is identified. Feedback globally heats the ICM and offsets cooling but also promotes local thermal instabilities via shocks, mixing, turbulence, and uplift.
AI.conclusion: AGN kinetic feedback plays a dual role: it globally heats the ICM to offset cooling while simultaneously creating conditions (compression, mixing, turbulence, uplift) that foster local thermal instability, fragmenting and redistributing cool gas without depleting it. High-resolution cosmological zoom-ins can capture the multiphase cool-core structure and its feedback coupling.

title: Nonlinear models of Mira variables with long secondary periods
comment: 11 pages, 6 figures, accepted to Astronomy Letters
summary: Calculations of nonlinear radial oscillations in asymptotic giant branch stars with an initial mass of $M_\mathrm{ZAMS}=1.6M_\odot$ were performed for initial helium and metal abundances of $Y=0.28$ and $Z=0.006$, respectively. Several models from the evolutionary sequence after the 4th thermal pulse were used as initial conditions for the hydrodynamic equations describing stellar pulsations with long secondary periods. Using the discrete Fourier transform of the hydrodynamic solutions we show that long secondary periods appear in Mira variables pulsating simultaneously in the fundamental mode and first overtone with non-multiple periods. The relative deviation from multiplicity is $δ_\mathrmΠ\le 1.2\times 10^{-2}$ and is responsible for mode splitting into equally spaced frequency components, each of which is a standing wave with a free outer boundary. The cycle length of long secondary periods is nearly 20 times that of the fundamental mode. Long secondary periodicity is a nonlinear effect that arises after reaching the limiting amplitude and develops over several hundred fundamental mode periods.

AI.tldr: Nonlinear radial pulsations of a 1.6 M⊙ AGB star are modeled; long secondary periods (LSPs) emerge when fundamental and first-overtone modes with non-commensurate periods interact, producing split, equally spaced frequency components.
AI.motivation: Long secondary periods in Mira variables lack a clear physical explanation; the authors test whether they can arise intrinsically from nonlinear mode interaction in asymptotic giant branch pulsations.
AI.method: Hydrodynamic simulations of nonlinear radial oscillations for an AGB star (M_ZAMS = 1.6 M⊙, Y = 0.28, Z = 0.006) were run, using models after the 4th thermal pulse as initial conditions. Discrete Fourier transforms of the solutions were analyzed to characterize the long secondary periodicity.
AI.result: LSPs appear in Miras pulsating simultaneously in the fundamental mode and first overtone with non-multiple (non-commensurate) periods; the departure from multiplicity is δ_Π ≤ 1.2×10⁻², splitting each mode into equally spaced frequency components, each a standing wave with a free outer boundary. The LSP cycle is ~20 times the fundamental period.
AI.conclusion: Long secondary periodicity is a nonlinear effect that arises after the limiting amplitude is reached and develops over several hundred fundamental-mode periods, providing a self-consistent intrinsic mechanism for LSPs in Mira variables.

title: Low-excitation molecular gas in a Ly$α$-associated companion of the $z=4.7$ quasar in BR1202-0725
comment: Submitted to A&A; 10 pages
summary: Quasar companions at high redshifts are usually gas-rich star-forming galaxies whose molecular gas masses ($M_{\mathrm{mol}}$) are estimated from [C II], dust emission or a single mid-$J$ CO line. We detect CO(5-4) and [C I](1-0) with ALMA in LAE-2, a Ly$α$-associated companion of the $z=4.7$ quasar in BR1202-0725, and CO(5-4) at the location near LAE-1, the Ly$α$ emitter between the quasar and the submillimeter galaxy (SMG). With the CO(2-1) flux from the literature, LAE-2 has an $L'_{\mathrm{CO(5-4)}}/L'_{\mathrm{CO(2-1)}}$ ratio of $0.22\pm0.04$, as in high-redshift main-sequence galaxies but four times lower than in the quasar host and the SMG. A non-LTE model places the CO(5-4) excitation temperature only 4 K above the cosmic microwave background (CMB), yet the same gas would show an even lower ratio against the $z=0$ CMB. The CMB-corrected $M_{\mathrm{mol}}$ from [C I], $\approx9\times10^{10} M_{\odot}$, agrees with the independent [C II] estimate, whereas CO(5-4) gives a four times lower mass if assumed thermalized at 40 K with the same CO-to-H$_2$ conversion factor. Combining our 3 mm measurement with archival far-infrared photometry, we find cold ($\approx25$ K) dust and main-sequence star formation, with a gas-to-stellar mass ratio of $\approx4$ and a depletion time of $\approx0.7$ Gyr. Its star formation can supply the far-ultraviolet field that the [C I], [C II], and CO lines require. Quasar companions can thus retain massive, weakly excited molecular gas reservoirs that mid-$J$ CO surveys can miss.

AI.tldr: ALMA CO(5-4) and [C I](1-0) observations of a Lyα companion (LAE-2) to the z=4.7 BR1202-0725 quasar reveal a massive, cold, weakly excited molecular gas reservoir that single mid-J CO estimates underestimate by ~4×, while [C I] and [C II] agree.
AI.motivation: Molecular gas masses of high-z quasar companions are typically derived from [C II], dust, or a single mid-J CO line, but such tracers may miss weakly excited gas and bias mass estimates. The authors test this by directly characterizing the excitation and mass of the molecular gas in a known Lyα companion.
AI.method: ALMA detects CO(5-4) and [C I](1-0) toward LAE-2 (and CO(5-4) near LAE-1) in the BR1202-0725 field at z=4.7. The authors combine these with literature CO(2-1) flux, apply a non-LTE excitation model including CMB effects, compare CO-derived masses to [C I] and [C II], and pair the 3 mm data with archival FIR photometry to constrain dust temperature, SFR, gas-to-stellar mass ratio, and depletion time.
AI.result: LAE-2 shows L'_CO(5-4)/L'_CO(2-1) = 0.22±0.04, matching high-z main-sequence galaxies but ~4× lower than the quasar host and SMG. Non-LTE modeling puts the CO(5-4) excitation temperature only ~4 K above the CMB. The CMB-corrected [C I] mass (~9×10^10 M☉) agrees with [C II], whereas CO(5-4) yields a 4× lower mass under thermalized 40 K assumptions. Dust is cold (~25 K) with main-sequence star formation, gas-to-stellar mass ratio ~4, and depletion time ~0.7 Gyr; the UV field from star formation can power the observed lines.
AI.conclusion: Quasar companions can harbor massive, weakly excited molecular gas that single mid-J CO surveys may underestimate; multi-line/[C I] observations with CMB corrections are needed for reliable gas masses in such systems.

title: Robustness of Transition Probabilities of Spectral Lines Deduced from Spatially Resolved Solar Spectra
comment: Accepted for publication in A&A; abstract abridged for arxiv; 15 pages
summary: Atomic parameters are a key ingredient for the synthesis of spectral lines to model observed spectra and to extract meaningful physical information about the observed astrophysical object. We use quiet-sun observations to test the reliability of the atomic parameter inference from observed spectra. Our focus is on the transition probability of spectral lines, denoted as log(gf). We apply a spectropolarimetric inversion method to quiet-sun disc-centre observations at 1.56 $μ$m from the GRIS/GREGOR spectrograph. We use the coupled method implemented in the globin inversion code, where atomic parameters are spatially coupled, and a single value of these parameters is determined for every spectral line over the entire field of view. We carry out tests to determine the sensitivity of the inferred log(gf) values to various atmospheric parameters and the data reduction fallibility. We find that our log(gf) values are weaker by 0.023 dex compared to the most recent study. This is most probably caused by the constraint imposed on the log(gf) parameter due to the spatial coupling, lifting the degeneracy between temperature and log(gf). We use the Markov chain Monte Carlo method to determine the uncertainty in the inferred log(gf) values. For the strongest lines in the spectral region, the uncertainty in log(gf) is 1-4 %, increasing to 12 % for weaker and blended lines. Our tests suggest that the log(gf) values inferred using the coupled method from globin are robust against any local contamination to the observed line profiles, such as spectral stray light, and return a reliable and unique set of log(gf) values for the strongest lines irrespective of the chosen atmospheric model and observation dataset. This result is valid as long as the underlying assumptions of line formation under local thermodynamic equilibrium and the completeness of the line list are satisfied.

AI.tldr: Using quiet-sun disc-centre spectropolarimetric observations at 1.56 μm, the authors infer transition probabilities log(gf) via globin's spatially coupled inversion and assess their reliability, uncertainties, and robustness against model and data-reduction choices.
AI.motivation: Atomic parameters such as log(gf) are essential for spectral synthesis and for extracting physical information about observed astrophysical objects, yet their reliability needs independent verification against real observations.
AI.method: Spectropolarimetric inversion of quiet-sun disc-centre observations at 1.56 μm from GRIS/GREGOR, using the globin code's coupled method in which atomic parameters are spatially coupled to yield one log(gf) value per line over the full field of view; sensitivity tests on atmospheric parameters and data-reduction fallibility, plus MCMC for uncertainty estimation.
AI.result: Inferred log(gf) values are weaker by 0.023 dex than the most recent study, likely because spatial coupling constrains log(gf) and lifts the temperature–log(gf) degeneracy. MCMC uncertainties are 1–4% for the strongest lines and up to 12% for weaker, blended lines. Tests indicate robustness against local contamination (e.g., stray light) and consistency across atmospheric models and datasets for strong lines.
AI.conclusion: The coupled globin method returns reliable, unique log(gf) values for the strongest lines irrespective of atmospheric model or observation dataset, valid under the assumptions of LTE line formation and a complete line list.

title: Euclid: Discovery of a quasar at z = 8.13 hosting a 360-million-solar-mass black hole
comment: Published in Astronomy & Astrophysics, Volume 715, Article A356 on November 24, 2026
summary: Quasars powered by rapid accretion onto supermassive black holes (SMBHs) have been uncovered deep into the first gigayear of cosmic history. We present the discovery of EUCL J150452.291+625224.39 (J1504+6252), selected from Euclid Wide Survey imaging and spectroscopically confirmed as the first quasar at z > 8 through observations with Keck, HST, LBT, and JWST. J1504+6252 exhibits the defining spectral signatures of archetypal quasars at lower redshift, including a luminous blue power-law continuum and broad permitted emission lines, indicating a classical broad-line region. JWST/NIRSpec G395M spectroscopy yields a systemic redshift of z = 8.129 +/- 0.005, corresponding to 630 Myr after the Big Bang and shifting the quasar redshift frontier by about 39 Myr (6% of the age of the Universe at that epoch). From H-beta and Mg II, we measured intrinsic broad-line-region FWHM of 3160 +/- 270 and 3740 (+160/-170) km/s, respectively. A widely used single-epoch H-beta calibration gives a reference black hole mass of log10(MBH/Msun) = 8.56 +/- 0.43. Applying a range of calibrations to both Mg II and H-beta yields log10(MBH/Msun) = 8.33-8.89 and Eddington ratios of 0.12-0.44. Assembling a black hole of several hundred million solar masses within the first few hundred million years, despite its currently sub-Eddington accretion rate, requires either a massive seed or sustained, highly efficient early growth. The discovery of a mature, sub-Eddington quasar at z > 8 suggests that substantially more luminous quasars hosting similarly massive black holes may remain to be discovered. Conversely, previously known reionisation-era quasars may represent the rapidly accreting end of a broader population of already massive black holes spanning a wider range of accretion states.

AI.tldr: Discovery of J1504+6252, the first spectroscopically confirmed quasar at z > 8 (z = 8.129), showing a mature broad-line region and a ~360 million solar-mass black hole accreting at sub-Eddington rates only ~630 Myr after the Big Bang.
AI.motivation: Rapidly accreting quasars are known deep into the first gigayear, but the redshift frontier for confirmed quasars and the diversity of accretion states among early massive black holes remain poorly constrained; pushing to z > 8 tests early black hole seeding and growth models.
AI.method: Selection from Euclid Wide Survey imaging, followed by spectroscopic confirmation with Keck, HST, LBT, and JWST. JWST/NIRSpec G395M spectroscopy provides the systemic redshift. Black hole masses are estimated from single-epoch broad-line (H-beta and Mg II) FWHM and continuum luminosity using multiple calibrations, yielding Eddington ratios.
AI.result: Systemic redshift z = 8.129 +/- 0.005 (630 Myr after the Big Bang), advancing the quasar frontier by ~39 Myr. Broad H-beta and Mg II FWHM of 3160 +/- 270 and 3740 (+160/-170) km/s. Reference H-beta mass log10(MBH/Msun) = 8.56 +/- 0.43; across calibrations 8.33-8.89, with Eddington ratios 0.12-0.44 (sub-Eddington). The object shows a luminous blue power-law continuum and broad permitted lines typical of lower-redshift quasars.
AI.conclusion: Assembling several hundred million solar masses within a few hundred Myr despite sub-Eddington accretion requires either a massive seed or sustained highly efficient early growth. A mature sub-Eddington quasar at z > 8 implies more luminous analogues may await discovery, and known reionisation-era quasars may represent only the rapidly accreting tail of a broader massive black hole population spanning diverse accretion states.

title: The evolution of discs and the epoch of formation of giant planets around low-mass stars
comment: 12 pages, 13 figures, 4 appendices with tables and figures
summary: Large-grain depletion in the inner discs of young stellar systems provides a potential observational signature of dust filtration by forming giant-planet cores. In a previous study, we found that $0.50\pm0.10$ of prominent protoplanetary discs around solar-type stars ($0.7$--$1.5$~\Msun) with ages of 2--8~Myr show evidence for a depletion of large grains inside the snow line. Such a depletion may arise when a sufficiently massive planetary core acts as a barrier to the inward drift of large grains, filtering them from the inner disc. If this interpretation is correct, the frequency of dust-filtration signatures should decrease towards lower stellar masses, in accordance with the lower occurrence rate of giant planets around low-mass stars. Extending our analysis to lower-mass stars, we found that only $0.09\pm0.09$ of discs around stars with masses of $0.30$--$0.58$~\Msun, corresponding to the progenitors of main-sequence early M-type stars, show evidence of grain filtration. This fraction is lower than that measured for solar-type stars and is consistent with the lower frequency of giant planets around M-type stars. We also found that discs exhibiting evidence of filtration tend to have relatively massive outer dust reservoirs, with dust masses exceeding $20$~\MEarth. Conversely, the absence of filtration signatures in lower-mass discs suggests that Neptune-mass and lower-mass planets, despite being common around low-mass stars, may generally be unable to filter large grains efficiently.

AI.tldr: Dust-filtration signatures (large-grain depletion inside the snow line) appear in 0.09±0.09 of discs around 0.30–0.58 Msun (early-M) stars, versus 0.50±0.10 for 0.7–1.5 Msun stars, consistent with the lower giant-planet frequency around lower-mass stars.
AI.motivation: Large-grain depletion in inner discs may be an observational signature of dust filtration by a forming giant-planet core. If so, the incidence of this signature should scale with stellar mass, mirroring the lower occurrence of giant planets around low-mass stars. The authors extend their prior survey of solar-type stars down to early M-type progenitors to test this prediction.
AI.method: Extends the earlier inner-disc grain-depletion analysis to protoplanetary discs around stars of 0.30–0.58 Msun (ages ~2–8 Myr), measuring the fraction showing large-grain depletion inside the snow line and comparing it with the 0.50±0.10 fraction previously found for 0.7–1.5 Msun stars. Disc dust masses are also compared between systems with and without filtration signatures.
AI.result: Only 0.09±0.09 of the lower-mass discs show evidence of grain filtration, significantly below the solar-type value and consistent with the lower giant-planet frequency around M stars. Discs exhibiting filtration tend to have massive outer dust reservoirs, with dust masses exceeding 20 MEarth. The absence of the signature in lower-mass discs suggests Neptune-mass and lower-mass planets, although common around low-mass stars, generally cannot efficiently filter large grains.
AI.conclusion: The stellar-mass dependence of dust-filtration signatures supports the interpretation that inner-disc large-grain depletion traces giant-planet cores. Efficient filtering appears to require cores massive enough to act as barriers and relatively dust-rich outer discs (>20 MEarth); Neptune-mass planets are likely insufficient.

title: The hot circumgalactic medium: implications of mixing and resolution at the disk-halo interface
comment: 19 pages, 7 figures. Submitted to ApJ
summary: We demonstrate that microphysical processes at the disk--halo interface, typically unresolved in circumgalactic medium (CGM) simulations, strongly affect the thermodynamic structure and observational signatures of an inflowing hot ($\sim10^6\,{\rm K}$) CGM. If the hot gas is pulled through the interface faster than it can cool, e.g.\ by turbulent mixing with the ISM or fountain flows, the hot CGM approaches an isentropic state. If instead the interface is regulated by radiative cooling on the hot gas cooling time, the hot CGM develops an outward-increasing entropy profile akin to a classic cooling flow. The two regimes differ by a factor of $\sim\!10$ in the predicted hot gas density above the disk near the rotation axis, and consequently by a factor of $\sim100$ in the predicted X-ray emission measure. We show that an isentropic CGM is produced in idealized CGM simulations that fail to resolve the pc-scale disk--halo interface, as numerical mixing drives artificially rapid cooling at the interface. A similar isentropic structure is found along the rotation axis in FIRE zoom-in simulations of $z\sim0$ Milky-Way-mass galaxies, where the cooling layer is likewise unresolved, raising the possibility that numerical mixing contributes to the isentropic structure. In contrast, an outward-increasing entropy profile forms in our idealized simulations when we replace the unresolved interface with an inner boundary that enforces a slow inflow. This outward-increasing entropy profile is likely also present in the Milky Way hot CGM, inferred from comparing density estimates at $\sim100\,{\rm kpc}$ with the entropy of the eROSITA bubbles.

AI.tldr: Unresolved disk–halo interface microphysics controls whether an inflowing hot CGM becomes isentropic or develops a cooling-flow entropy profile, changing predicted densities by ~10x and X-ray emission by ~100x.
AI.motivation: The pc-scale disk–halo interface is unresolved in CGM simulations, so its microphysics are treated numerically rather than physically. The authors aim to show that these unresolved processes strongly affect the thermodynamic structure and observables of hot (~10^6 K) inflowing CGM.
AI.method: They contrast two interface regimes: rapid pulling of hot gas through the interface (turbulent mixing with the ISM or fountain flows) yielding an isentropic hot CGM, versus an interface regulated by radiative cooling on the hot-gas cooling time yielding an outward-increasing entropy profile like a classic cooling flow. They test this with idealized CGM simulations, compare to FIRE zoom-in simulations of z~0 Milky-Way-mass galaxies, and replace the unresolved interface with an inner boundary enforcing slow inflow. They also infer the Milky Way profile by comparing density estimates at ~100 kpc with eROSITA bubble entropy.
AI.result: The two regimes differ by a factor ~10 in hot gas density above the disk near the rotation axis and by ~100 in predicted X-ray emission measure. Idealized CGM simulations that fail to resolve the interface produce an isentropic CGM because numerical mixing drives artificially rapid cooling. FIRE zoom-in simulations show a similar isentropic structure along the rotation axis where the cooling layer is unresolved. Replacing the unresolved interface with a slow-inflow inner boundary instead produces an outward-increasing entropy profile.
AI.conclusion: Interface microphysics, not resolved in standard simulations, determine the hot CGM entropy structure and its X-ray signatures; numerical mixing may artificially enforce isentropy. The outward-increasing entropy profile expected physically is likely also present in the Milky Way hot CGM, consistent with density estimates at ~100 kpc and eROSITA bubble entropy.

title: Photometric Characterisation and Evolutionary State Investigation of the Low Mass-Ratio Contact Binary FASTT 1558
comment: 24 pages, 13 figures, 9 tables, accepted for publication in ApJ
summary: Contact binaries with low mass ratios, as potential progenitors of stellar mergers, offer important insights into the physical processes governing mass and energy transfer. In this work, we present the first spectro-photometry based evolutionary investigation of FASTT 1558, a totally eclipsing, low mass-ratio contact binary. We combine TESS and ASAS-SN photometry with phase-resolved spectroscopy obtained with the 3.6m Devasthal Optical Telescope. The lightcurve modeling with PHOEBE shows that the system has an exceptionally low secondary-to-primary mass ratio of $q=0.1544\pm0.0013$, with a deep contact degree of $f=0.61\pm0.01$. Our analysis yields a total system mass of $1.92\pm0.31\,M_\odot$, while the distance to the system is estimated to be $648.45\pm29.85$ pc. Analysis of long-term eclipse timings reveals an apparent orbital period decrease of $\dot{P}=-(3.03\pm0.26) \times 10^{-7}$ ${\rm day\,yr^{-1}}$, which may be associated with mass-transfer from the primary to the secondary on a thermal timescale. The spectra show phase-dependent H$α$ and CaII equivalent widths, indicating a dynamically evolving chromosphere. Binary evolution calculations with MESA terminates through L2 overflow before reaching the observed low mass-ratio. Despite its extreme mass ratio, the system is presently Darwin stable, with $J_{\rm spin}/J_{\rm orb}=0.15\pm0.02$. FASTT 1558 therefore provides a robust observational benchmark for evolutionary models of low mass-ratio contact binaries.

AI.tldr: First spectro-photometric evolutionary study of the totally eclipsing contact binary FASTT 1558, revealing an extremely low mass ratio (q≈0.154), deep contact, and orbital period decrease likely driven by thermal-timescale mass transfer.
AI.motivation: Low mass-ratio contact binaries are potential progenitors of stellar mergers, and understanding their mass/energy transfer physics requires well-characterized observational benchmarks with both photometry and phase-resolved spectroscopy.
AI.method: Combined TESS and ASAS-SN photometry with phase-resolved spectroscopy from the 3.6m Devasthal Optical Telescope; lightcurve modeling with PHOEBE; long-term eclipse timing (O-C) analysis; spectral line analysis of H-alpha and CaII equivalent widths; MESA binary evolution calculations; Darwin stability assessment via spin-to-orbital angular momentum ratio.
AI.result: Derived secondary-to-primary mass ratio q=0.1544±0.0013, contact degree f=0.61±0.01, total mass 1.92±0.31 M_sun, distance 648.45±29.85 pc. Eclipse timings show period decrease of P_dot=-(3.03±0.26)×10^-7 day/yr, consistent with primary-to-secondary mass transfer on a thermal timescale. Phase-dependent H-alpha and CaII equivalent widths indicate a dynamical chromosphere. MESA evolution terminates via L2 overflow before reaching the observed low q. System is Darwin stable with J_spin/J_orb=0.15±0.02.
AI.conclusion: FASTT 1558 is a robust observational benchmark for evolutionary models of low mass-ratio contact binaries, being Darwin stable despite its extreme mass ratio, while standard MESA models fail to reproduce the observed low q (terminating through L2 overflow).

title: The SDSS-V Black Hole Mapper Reverberation Mapping Project: Time-delayed Variability of a Quasar's C IV Broad Absorption Troughs
comment: 29 pages, 24 figures, 4 tables
summary: Broad absorption line (BAL) quasars offer a powerful view into the structure, kinematics, and feedback mechanics of active galactic nuclei. In this study, we track the dramatic behavior of intrinsic CIV outflows of the quasar SDSS J142129.40+522752.0 at z = 3.228. We analyze 199 high-signal- to-noise optical spectra collected over a 12-year baseline via the Sloan Digital Sky Survey III/IV Reverberation Mapping and the SDSS-V Black Hole Mapper Reverberation Mapping programs. We quantify multi-year variability across two prominent absorption features: a primary high-velocity CIV BAL trough (Trough A) and a lower-velocity mini-BAL (Trough B). Both troughs exhibit rapid, significant variations in equivalent width and average depth, culminating in temporary disappearances during the 2022-2023 observing seasons before reappearing at their original velocities. We find that the behavior of the two troughs is highly correlated with both the g-band flux and each other, strongly indicating that the observed variability is driven by ionization state changes of the gas. The equivalent width of the mini-BAL Trough B is found to lag that of Trough A by ~4 days in the quasar rest frame, suggesting that the equilibrium timescales of the two absorbers are different and possibly indicative of different outflow densities or distances.

AI.tldr: Highly correlated, ionization-driven variability of two CIV outflows in quasar SDSS J142129.40+522752.0, with the mini-BAL lagging the primary BAL by ~4 rest-frame days.
AI.motivation: BAL quasars probe AGN structure, kinematics, and feedback, but the physical driver (density, distance, ionization) behind outflow variability is poorly constrained; long-baseline, high-S/N monitoring can disentangle these.
AI.method: Analyzed 199 high-S/N optical spectra of SDSS J142129.40+522752.0 (z = 3.228) over a 12-year baseline from SDSS-III/IV RM and SDSS-V BHM RM; measured equivalent width and mean depth variability of a high-velocity CIV BAL (Trough A) and a lower-velocity mini-BAL (Trough B), and cross-correlated with g-band flux and between troughs.
AI.result: Both troughs show rapid, significant EW and depth changes; they disappear in the 2022–2023 seasons and reappear at the same velocities. Variability is strongly correlated between troughs and with g-band flux. Trough B lags Trough A by ~4 days (rest frame).
AI.conclusion: Outflow variability is driven by ionization-state changes of the absorbing gas. The ~4-day lag implies different equilibrium/recombination timescales, plausibly reflecting different outflow densities or distances for the two absorbers.

title: A catalog of Gaia DR3 luminous blue variables and candidate luminous blue variables
comment: 18 pages, 11 figures
summary: Galactic LBVs are rare, evolved massive stars whose defining evidence is long-term spectroscopic and photometric instability, including S Doradus-type cycles, and, in exceptional cases, giant eruptions. Candidate LBVs (cLBVs) share LBV-like spectra and/or circumstellar nebulae; however, they lack long-term observational datasets that would detect their long-term variability and confirm their classification as bona fide LBVs. Modern time-domain surveys provide homogeneous light curves for many Galactic massive stars, but each survey has its own limitations in terms of depth, temporal coverage, and observing cadence. Using confirmed Galactic LBVs as a control sample, we aim to test what Gaia DR3 and complementary photometric surveys can and cannot establish about LBV-type variability. We assembled a vetted sample of 75 Galactic LBVs and cLBVs with near- and mid-infrared photometry from 2MASS, MSX, WISE, GLIMPSE, and MIPSGAL. The infrared material was used to validate identifications, evaluate source confusion, and place objects in a circumstellar-dust context. We then constructed light curves from Gaia DR3, the Bochum survey, the ASAS SN, and the ZTF, and analyzed large-amplitude and periodic cases with Lomb-Scargle (LS) and phase dispersion minimization (PDM) methods. Gaia DR3 matches are available for 67% of the sample and 76% are reported as variable. We identify high-amplitude variables and periodic systems that may be binaries rather than classical LBVs. Six confirmed LBVs and five candidates show variations larger than 0.6 mag in the Gaia RP filter. Their light curves are examined and three periodic variables are identified. The light curves of OMN2000 LS1 and DWC2011 140 show primary and secondary minima, strongly suggesting eclipsing binary systems. OMN2000 LS1 has a well-constrained period of 80.29 d, and DWC2011 140 of 95.07 d.

AI.tldr: A vetted sample of 75 Galactic LBVs and candidate LBVs is analyzed with multi-survey IR and optical photometry (Gaia DR3, Bochum, ASAS-SN, ZTF) to test what these datasets can establish about LBV-type variability; results include high-amplitude variables and three periodic systems, two of which are likely eclipsing binaries.
AI.motivation: Galactic LBVs are rare and defined by long-term spectroscopic and photometric instability, but candidate LBVs lack the long-term datasets needed to confirm their classification. Modern time-domain surveys offer homogeneous light curves yet differ in depth, cadence, and temporal coverage, so their diagnostic power for LBV variability needs systematic evaluation.
AI.method: Compiled a vetted sample of 75 Galactic LBVs and cLBVs with near- and mid-IR photometry from 2MASS, MSX, WISE, GLIMPSE, and MIPSGAL, used to validate identifications, assess source confusion, and contextualize circumstellar dust. Constructed light curves from Gaia DR3, the Bochum survey, ASAS-SN, and ZTF, and analyzed large-amplitude and periodic cases using Lomb-Scargle and phase dispersion minimization (PDM).
AI.result: Gaia DR3 matches exist for 67% of the sample and 76% are reported variable. High-amplitude variables and periodic systems that may be binaries rather than classical LBVs are identified; six confirmed LBVs and five candidates vary by more than 0.6 mag in Gaia RP. Three periodic variables are found, with OMN2000 LS1 and DWC2011 140 showing primary and secondary minima indicative of eclipsing binaries (periods of 80.29 d and 95.07 d, respectively).
AI.conclusion: Current survey photometry can detect large-amplitude LBV-like variability and reveal contaminants, but long-term multi-survey light curves are essential; some apparent high-amplitude or periodic cLBVs are likely eclipsing binaries rather than bona fide LBVs, underscoring the need for continued spectroscopic and photometric monitoring to secure classifications.

title: H$_3^+$ forbidden rotational lines in a planetary nebula: JWST/MIRI detection in the Ring Nebula and ionization by the central star
comment: Accepted for publication in ApJ Letters. 13 pages, 5 figures, 1 table. Primary category: astro-ph.GA (cross-list: astro-ph.SR, physics.chem-ph). License: arXiv perpetual, non-exclusive license (the default; compatible with the AAS copyright agreement)
summary: We report the detection of the forbidden pure rotational spectrum of H$_3^+$ in the Ring Nebula (NGC 6720), to our knowledge the first detection of H$_3^+$ in a planetary nebula. In JWST/MIRI spectra obtained toward the inner edge of the main ring, 0.1 pc in projection from the central star, the $(J,K) = (5,0)\to(4,3)$ line at 16.325 $μ$m is detected at $32σ$, along with nine further unblended lines. The H$_3^+$ emission spatially follows the H$_2$ emission, whose rotational lines show warm (660 K) and hot (1700 K) components. A statistical-equilibrium model at these temperatures reproduces the subthermal H$_3^+$ line pattern, with much of the emission arising in the hot H$_2$. The emission requires an H$_2$ ionization rate of $\sim 3\times 10^{-12}\,{\rm s^{-1}}$ in the hot H$_2$ for an electron fraction of $2\times 10^{-4}$. The rate is $\sim 2\times 10^4$ times the cosmic-ray ionization rate in diffuse clouds. The extreme-ultraviolet and soft X-ray radiation (54-300 eV) of the 135 kK central star supplies this rate if the hot H$_2$ lies within an H-nucleus column density of (4-8)$\times 10^{19}\,{\rm cm^{-2}}$ of the ionization front of the dense globules. Static photoionization models, however, place the H$_2$ in gas too cold to excite the H$_3^+$ lines. The warm molecular gas and its H$_3^+$ thus suggest dynamical effects, most plausibly the advection of H$_2$ through a photoevaporation front into gas heated by the star. H$_3^+$ provides a new probe of the photoionization of molecular gas by very hot stars.

AI.tldr: First detection of H3+ in a planetary nebula (Ring Nebula, NGC 6720), via JWST/MIRI forbidden rotational lines at 16.3 μm, revealing highly ionized warm/hot molecular gas driven by the hot central star and requiring dynamical photoevaporation.
AI.motivation: H3+ is a fundamental molecular ion and sensitive probe of ionization and chemistry in molecular gas, but it had never been detected in a planetary nebula. The authors aim to detect it in the Ring Nebula and use it to constrain the ionization of molecular gas irradiated by a very hot central star.
AI.method: JWST/MIRI spectroscopy of the inner edge of the main ring (0.1 pc projected from the central star). Detection of the (J,K)=(5,0)→(4,3) line at 16.325 μm at 32σ plus nine unblended lines; comparison with H2 rotational lines (warm 660 K and hot 1700 K components) and a statistical-equilibrium excitation model.
AI.result: H3+ emission spatially follows H2 emission; a statistical-equilibrium model at 660/1700 K reproduces the subthermal line pattern, with most emission arising in the hot H2. Requires an H2 ionization rate ~3×10^-12 s^-1 (for electron fraction 2×10^-4), ~2×10^4 times the diffuse-cloud cosmic-ray ionization rate. The 135 kK central star's EUV/soft X-ray (54–300 eV) radiation supplies this rate if hot H2 lies within an H-nucleus column of (4–8)×10^19 cm^-2 of the ionization front of dense globules.
AI.conclusion: Static photoionization models place the H2 too cold to excite H3+, so the warm molecular gas and its H3+ imply dynamical effects—most plausibly advection of H2 through a photoevaporation front into star-heated gas. H3+ is established as a new probe of molecular-gas photoionization by very hot stars.

title: Constraining the Binary Fraction and Mass-Ratio Distribution of FGK Dwarfs with Gaia XP Spectra: Metallicity, $α$-Element, and Age Dependencies
comment: 24 pages, 17 figures plus 1 online figure set with 2 additional figures, 5 tables, accepted for publication in ApJ
summary: We present a study of the binary fraction and mass-ratio distribution for near 200,000 FGK dwarf stars within 1 kpc, utilizing the Stellar Locus Outlier (SLOT) method applied to synthetic Gaia XP photometry and stellar parameters from LAMOST DR9. By modeling the asymmetric color residuals relative to a metallicity-dependent single-star locus, we measure the binary fraction $f_b$ and constrain the power-law slope $γ_{\rm large\,q}$ of the mass-ratio distribution at high mass ratio $q$. Higher metallicity is associated with a steeper (more negative) $γ_{{\rm large}q}$, indicating a larger proportion of low-mass-ratio systems. For $α$-elements, [Mg/H] and [Si/H] are anticorrelated with $f_b$ in thin-disk-dominated subsamples; conversely, [Ca/H] shows a positive correlation with $f_b$ in thin-disk-dominated subsamples. No correlation is found between $f_b$ and $α$-element abundances in thick-disk-dominated subsamples. The binary fraction increases modestly toward older ages in the thin-disk population, a trend that likely reflects underlying correlations with chemistry. Our results shed light on how chemical composition and dynamical processes shape the binary properties of solar-type stars.

AI.tldr: Using the Stellar Locus Outlier method on synthetic Gaia XP photometry plus LAMOST DR9 parameters, the binary fraction and mass-ratio slope of ~200,000 FGK dwarfs within 1 kpc are measured and linked to metallicity, alpha-element abundances, and age.
AI.motivation: The binary fraction and mass-ratio distribution of solar-type stars encode how star formation and dynamical processing depend on chemical composition; a large, homogeneous sample with chemical abundances is needed to test these dependencies.
AI.method: The Stellar Locus Outlier (SLOT) method is applied to synthetic Gaia XP photometry with LAMOST DR9 stellar parameters for ~200,000 FGK dwarfs within 1 kpc. Asymmetric color residuals relative to a metallicity-dependent single-star locus are modeled to derive the binary fraction f_b and the power-law slope gamma_large_q of the mass-ratio distribution at high q; trends are examined versus metallicity, [Mg/H], [Si/H], [Ca/H], and age, split by thin- vs thick-disk dominance.
AI.result: Higher metallicity yields a steeper (more negative) gamma_large_q, i.e., more low-mass-ratio systems. In thin-disk-dominated subsamples, [Mg/H] and [Si/H] anticorrelate with f_b while [Ca/H] correlates positively; no f_b–alpha-element correlation appears in thick-disk-dominated subsamples. The binary fraction rises modestly with age in the thin disk.
AI.conclusion: Chemical composition and dynamical processes jointly shape the binary properties of solar-type stars, with the age trend in f_b likely reflecting underlying chemistry correlations rather than a purely dynamical origin.

title: Clumping Factor in the Mix: Incomplete Mixing Suppresses Turbulent Reaction Boost
comment: 16 pages, 10 figures, submitted; comments welcome
summary: Cosmological simulations often account for unresolved density fluctuations using a sub-grid clumping factor when modeling chemical reactions. To validate this approach, we conduct hydrodynamical simulations of isothermal, supersonic turbulence and track the evolution of passive chemical species in first-, second-, and third-order reactions, exploring seven reaction rates across Mach numbers $M$ = 2-50 in three turbulence driving modes. We parametrize the saturation of clumping factors at $M \gtrsim 10$ due to intermittency (i.e., falling significantly below the log-normal prediction) with a one-parameter fitting formula. Furthermore, we find that the competition between turbulent mixing and the density-dependent reaction rates, governed by the Damköhler number (Da), suppresses the global reaction rate by a \textit{mixing efficiency} factor ($ξ$). For Da $\ll 1$, chemical species remain well mixed ($ξ\to 1$), and the reaction rates are boosted by a clumping factor. For Da $\gg 1$, reactants in dense gas are rapidly depleted before being redistributed by turbulence, causing $ξ$ to drop by a factor of a few to more than an order of magnitude. We quantify the effective mixing efficiency as a function of two dimensionless parameters, $M$ and Da, and provide a fitting formula that can be easily adopted in cosmological simulations to accurately follow unresolved chemical reactions.

AI.tldr: Isothermal, supersonic turbulence simulations of passive chemical reactions show that clumping factors saturate below the log-normal prediction at M≳10 and that turbulence suppresses global reaction rates by a mixing-efficiency factor ξ, both captured by fitting formulas in terms of Mach number and Damköhler number for use in cosmological sub-grid models.
AI.motivation: Cosmological simulations model unresolved density fluctuations via a sub-grid clumping factor when treating chemical reactions; this approach needs validation, particularly regarding how turbulence and the competition between mixing and reaction rates affect effective reaction rates.
AI.method: Hydrodynamical simulations of isothermal, supersonic turbulence with three driving modes; tracking passive chemical species in first-, second-, and third-order reactions at seven reaction rates across Mach numbers M = 2-50; parametrizing clumping-factor saturation with a one-parameter formula; quantifying mixing efficiency ξ as a function of M and Damköhler number Da.
AI.result: Clumping factors saturate at M≳10 due to intermittency, falling significantly below the log-normal prediction. Global reaction rates are suppressed by ξ: for Da≪1 the gas stays well mixed (ξ→1) and rates are boosted by clumping, while for Da≫1 reactants in dense gas deplete before redistribution, reducing ξ by a few to over an order of magnitude.
AI.conclusion: The effective mixing efficiency is characterized as a function of M and Da, and a fitting formula is provided that can be readily adopted in cosmological simulations to more accurately follow unresolved chemical reactions.

title: The W Transform: an additional powerful tool for astrophysical time-series analysis
comment: 25 pages, 11 figures, accepted for publication in ApJ
summary: This work introduces the W Transform (WT) for astrophysical applications and explores its similarities and differences to the Continuous Wavelet Transform (CWT), in photometric stellar light curves (LCs). We tested both techniques on synthetic data, producing LCs with different noise levels and numbers of gaps, and applied them to LCs from TESS space mission. The analysis focused on six stars: the solar analog TIC 276293046, the ultra-cool dwarf TIC 359892714, the $γ$ Dor pulsator TIC 164173105, the eclipsing binary TIC 355151781, the hosting planet star TIC 142276270, and the brown dwarf TIC 102076870. Overall, the results were in agreement, except for stars with LCs presenting sector-to-sector differences in structures or changes in the number of gaps, reflecting time-dynamic effects in the same target, which affect how time-dependent variability features appear in the time-frequency representation. For such LCs, the WT spectra are more stable and accurate in recovering signal amplitudes than the CWT maps, which exhibit distortions and limitations, showing that the inherent flexibility of the WT method in adjusting the dominant frequency could enhance time resolution even in LCs with complex or variable structures. We conclude that the WT is a robust tool for the analysis of stellar LCs, and that both methods may complement each other in an in-depth analysis of a periodic astrophysical signal. The present results suggest that the WT is a robust and accurate tool for analyzing stellar LCs, expanding the range of numerical techniques available for analyzing different stellar periodic phenomena from photometric observations.

AI.tldr: The W Transform (WT) is introduced and benchmarked against the Continuous Wavelet Transform (CWT) for time-frequency analysis of TESS stellar light curves, showing comparable performance overall but superior stability and amplitude fidelity for variable/multi-sector targets.
AI.motivation: Photometric stellar light curves exhibit time-dependent, non-stationary variability (gaps, sector-to-sector structural changes), demanding time-frequency tools that resolve variability accurately; the paper assesses whether the WT is a viable and robust alternative/complement to the widely used CWT.
AI.method: Synthetic light curves with varying noise levels and gap fractions were generated and analyzed with both WT and CWT; the methods were then applied to TESS light curves of six stars spanning distinct variability classes (solar analog TIC 276293046, ultra-cool dwarf TIC 359892714, γ Dor pulsator TIC 164173105, eclipsing binary TIC 355151781, planet-host TIC 142276270, and brown dwarf TIC 102076870). Comparisons focused on time-frequency spectra, signal-amplitude recovery, and stability across sectors.
AI.result: WT and CWT results generally agreed. Discrepancies arose for stars whose light curves show sector-to-sector structural changes or varying gap counts, i.e., time-dynamic effects. In such cases WT spectra were more stable and recovered signal amplitudes more accurately, whereas CWT maps exhibited distortions and limitations; the WT's adaptive dominant-frequency adjustment yields improved time resolution even for complex or variable structures.
AI.conclusion: The WT is a robust and accurate tool for analyzing stellar light curves, extending the numerical toolkit for periodic stellar phenomena in photometric data; WT and CWT are best regarded as complementary for in-depth analysis of periodic astrophysical signals.

title: Electron processing of glycine: evidence for peptide-forming condensation reactions
comment: 9 pages, 5 main article figures, 4 appendix figures, to be submitted to A&A
summary: The discovery of amino acids on asteroids, including samples returned from asteroid Bennu, and the detection of glycine on comet 67P/Churyumov-Gerasimenko support the hypothesis that glycine can form in extraterrestrial environments. Laboratory experiments show that glycine can form through both energetic and non-energetic processing of interstellar ice analogues. In the interstellar medium, glycine is exposed to various forms of energetic processing, including cosmic rays and the secondary electrons they generate, which have been shown to produce complex organic molecules, including peptides. This work investigates whether peptide-forming chemistry is a general consequence of energetic processing. Films of glycine and glycine-d3 were grown in two ultrahigh-vacuum chambers and irradiated with 1-2 keV electrons. The irradiated samples were subsequently characterised using infrared spectroscopy, temperature-programmed desorption, and vacuum-ultraviolet spectroscopy. Peptide formation through condensation reactions would produce water as a secondary product, and spectra obtained following irradiation of glycine-d3 showed evidence of D2O formation, supported by TPD measurements, which revealed H2O formation for glycine and H2O, HDO, and D2O for glycine-d3. VUV spectra of irradiated glycine showed the formation of decomposition products, including CO and CO2, as well as H2O. Following heating, a non-volatile residue remained on the surface. Electron irradiation of glycine produces reaction products similar to proton irradiation, suggesting that the resulting chemistry is not strongly dependent on the energy source. These findings support the possibility that larger organic molecules can form in a wide range of extraterrestrial environments. Such molecules may subsequently be incorporated into small bodies and delivered to planetary surfaces, potentially contributing to the emergence of life.

AI.tldr: Electron irradiation (1–2 keV) of glycine and glycine-d3 ices in ultrahigh vacuum produces peptide-forming chemistry, evidenced by D2O/H2O, CO, CO2, and a non-volatile residue, indicating energetic processing generically drives peptide formation across extraterrestrial environments.
AI.motivation: Glycine has been detected on asteroids (including Bennu samples) and comet 67P, and laboratory ice analogues show it can form via energetic and non-energetic processing. In the ISM, glycine is exposed to cosmic rays and their secondary electrons, which are known to generate complex organics including peptides.
